alaskan-malamute: An Alaskan Malamute is a freight dog, not a husky with a quieter reputation. Plan on a heavy double coat, a strong pull on the leash, and heat intolerance once the temperature climbs. Hip dysplasia and inherited polyneuropathy are the screening questions for a breeder, and a fenced yard matters because this dog can drag a person.
australian-terrier: An Australian Terrier is a small working terrier with a harsh coat that needs stripping or combing, not a clipper shave. They bark at movement and they will hunt a rat in the yard. Patellar luxation and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease show up in the hind leg, so a limp is a vet visit rather than a rest day.
bearded-collie: A Bearded Collie carries a long double coat that mats down to the skin if it is brushed only on the surface. They are a herding dog with a real bark and a need to move. Addison's disease, low adrenal function, is the illness this breed is known for, and it can look like a vague stomach upset until a vet runs the test.

Daily Bearded Collie care is a line-brush of the coat, a long walk or herding game, and a watch on appetite and energy. A beard holds water and food, so wipe it after meals or the skin under the chin gets infected. A dog that is suddenly weak, vomiting, or unwilling to stand needs an adrenal test, not another day of rest.
beauceron: A Beauceron is a French herding dog the size of a large working breed, with double dewclaws on the hind legs and a suspicious streak toward strangers. They need a job and a handler who has already trained a powerful dog. Hip and elbow dysplasia, and bloat in a deep chest, are the medical risks to budget for.

A Beauceron day includes training, not just a lap of the block. They herd motion, including children and bikes, unless that behavior is directed. Feed them in a calm moment and do not exercise hard right after a meal, because large deep-chested dogs can bloat.
belgian-sheepdog: The Belgian Sheepdog, the Groenendael, is the long-haired black Belgian shepherd. They are high-drive, noise-sensitive, and poor kennel dogs. Hip dysplasia and epilepsy are the health questions to ask. A bored one will bark, pace, and invent a job that involves the cat. The coat mats if you only brush the surface, so line it out to the skin a few times a week.
boerboel: A Boerboel is a South African mastiff bred to hold a threat, not to greet the mail carrier. Adults are heavy, short-lived compared with a retriever, and capable of serious damage if the guarding instinct is untrained. Hip and elbow disease, entropion, and heart checks belong in the purchase conversation, and many insurers treat the breed as a restricted mastiff.
border-collie: A border collie that finishes a walk and still stares at the cat has not had a job. Two hours of training, herding, or running is a start, and a puzzle toy is a snack. Trapped neutrophil syndrome and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis are fatal and DNA-testable. Ask for those results, plus collie eye anomaly and hip scores, before the puppy is cute enough to skip them.
border-terrier: A Border Terrier is a small earthdog with an otter head and a wiry coat that should be hand-stripped, not shaved. They are sturdy for a terrier and still obsessed with a hole in the ground. Canine epileptoid cramping syndrome, sometimes called Spike's disease, causes episodic cramping that looks like a seizure and is worth naming to the vet.
bordoodle: A Bordoodle is a border collie crossed with a poodle, so the puppy may inherit the collie's need for a job, the poodle's coat, or both. Size and shedding are not predictable from the parents' photos. Ask what the coat actually does at a year old, and plan mental work every day even if the dog looks like a teddy bear.
briard: A Briard is a French herding dog under a long goat-like coat, with double dewclaws behind. The coat mats if it is not lined out to the skin, and the dog herds motion in the house. Hip dysplasia and bloat are the large-breed risks. This is a working dog that lives a long time if the coat and the brain both get daily attention.
bulldog: An English Bulldog cannot cool itself the way a long-nosed dog can. Snoring, heat, and exercise intolerance are airway disease, brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome, until a vet says otherwise. Skin-fold infections, cherry eye, and a back end that often needs a cesarean are the rest of the budget. Keep them lean and out of summer heat.
canaan-dog: A Canaan Dog is a Middle Eastern pariah breed: alert, reserved with strangers, and quick to bark at a change in the yard. They are not a soft retriever. They need a secure fence because they patrol, and they do better with a job than with being left as a lawn ornament. Heat is less of a problem than boredom.
cardigan-welsh-corgi: A Cardigan Welsh Corgi is the long-tailed, heavier corgi, still a dwarf herding dog with the same spinal risk. Intervertebral disc disease is why they should not jump off the couch or live overweight. They herd feet and they bark. A ramp, a lean body, and a real walk beat a flight of stairs.
caucasian-shepherd: A Caucasian Shepherd is a livestock guardian, often over 100 pounds, bred to work alone at night and to decide who does not belong. They are not a family mastiff for a first-time home. Barking, independence, and suspicion of guests are the breed, and hip disease plus a short giant-breed lifespan belong in the cost plan.
cavalier-king-charles: A Cavalier King Charles Spaniel's teeth crowd a short muzzle, and periodontal disease is painful long before the dog stops eating. Brush daily and expect dental cleanings. Mitral valve disease is common enough that a murmur in middle age is a cardiology plan, not a surprise, and an MRI is what separates syringomyelia from an ear infection when the dog scratches at the air.

Daily cavalier care is a short walk, a coat brush, tooth brushing, and a hand on the chest to learn that dog's normal heart. Keep them lean. Extra weight makes the airway and the heart work harder, and a cavalier that pants at rest in a cool room needs a vet, not a later bedtime.

Insurance for a cavalier is about the heart and the neck, not about accidents alone. Read whether cardiac disease and advanced imaging are covered, and enroll while the dog is young and the record is still clean. A policy bought after the murmur is written down will not pay for that heart.
cavalier-king-charles-spaniel: Cavalier King Charles Spaniels need a cardiologist's timeline, not only a groomer. Mitral valve disease becomes common with age, and syringomyelia can cause a phantom scratch at the neck or ear. Ask the breeder for heart and MRI or DNA screening details, keep the dog lean, and treat a new cough or air-scratch as medical.
chesapeake-bay-retriever: A Chesapeake Bay Retriever has an oily, water-resistant coat and a guarding streak that a Labrador usually does not. They were built to retrieve in cold water and to be possessive of a bird. Hip dysplasia is the orthopedic question. They need a job and a handler, and the coat should be washed, not stripped of the oil that protects it.
chinese-crested: A Chinese Crested is often hairless on the body, with a coat on the head, tail, and feet. Bare skin burns in sun and chills in air conditioning, and it needs washing, not shaving. Dental disease is severe because the hairless variety often has missing or crowded teeth. Patellar luxation is the knee problem to watch when a small dog skips.
dutch-shepherd: A Dutch Shepherd is a rare herding breed, usually brindle, with the same working drive people expect from a Malinois. They need sport, tracking, or a real job, and they are a poor choice for a home that wants a quiet yard dog. Hip screening matters, and a puppy with no outlet will bark and chew the work it was not given.
english-bulldog: An English Bulldog's face, skin folds, and hips are the care plan. Brachycephalic airway disease makes heat and exercise dangerous. Clean the facial folds so they do not yeast, keep the dog lean, and budget for cherry eye, skin infections, and often a cesarean. A bulldog wheezing in a warm room is an emergency, not a quirk of the breed.
german-shorthaired-pointer: A German Shorthaired Pointer is a versatile hunting dog that needs hours of running, not a weekend hike. They are affectionate and destructive when under-exercised. Hip dysplasia and a deep chest that can bloat are the medical budget. Do not feed a large meal and then run the dog. A GSP left alone all day will redesign the couch.
giant-schnauzer: A Giant Schnauzer is a working guard dog in a wiry coat, not a large miniature schnauzer. They need training, a job, and hand-stripping or a planned clip. Hip dysplasia and a strong defensive streak are the reasons this breed overwhelms a first dog home. Size alone makes an untrained one dangerous in a doorway.
ibizan-hound: An Ibizan Hound is a tall sighthound that hunts by sight and can clear a fence that would hold a Labrador. They are lean, sensitive to anesthesia, and rude about small animals. Give them a sprint in a secure area and a soft bed for the other twenty hours. Low body fat means they chill easily and they show ribs on purpose.
irish-water-spaniel: An Irish Water Spaniel wears a liver-colored curly coat with a rat tail and needs swimming or another hard job. The coat mats if it is not combed to the skin, and clipping without a plan ruins the waterproofing people bought the dog for. Hip dysplasia is common enough to ask for scores.

An Irish Water Spaniel day is coat work plus exercise that actually tires a spaniel. They are clowns at home and serious in water. Dry the coat after a swim so the skin does not stay wet under the curls, and keep the ear canals clean because floppy spaniel ears grow yeast.
japanese-chin: A Japanese Chin is a tiny brachycephalic companion, often under 10 pounds, with a flat face and a long coat. They overheat, they injure easily if dropped, and patellar luxation is the knee skip to have checked. They are a lap dog, not a jogging partner. Snoring that becomes open-mouth breathing in a cool room needs a vet.
japanese-spitz: A Japanese Spitz is a small white spitz with a stand-off coat that blows twice a year. They bark, they shed in clumps, and they are more companion than sled dog. Brush to the skin during the blow or the undercoat felts. Patellar luxation is the small-dog knee issue to mention at the wellness visit.

Daily care for a Japanese Spitz is a brush, a walk, and a plan for the bark. They are bright and they will announce every passerby. A crate or a quiet room helps if the dog is rehearsing the alarm all evening. Keep them lean so the patellas are not carrying extra weight.
manchester-terrier: A Manchester Terrier comes in standard and toy sizes, both sleek, short-coated, and built to hunt. They are not a soft lap dog even at toy weight. They need a run and a secure yard because prey drive does not retire. von Willebrand disease has been reported in the breed, so ask about clotting status before a surgery is scheduled.
norwich-terrier: A Norwich Terrier is the prick-eared cousin of the Norfolk, a small working terrier with a wiry coat. Upper airway syndrome is the breed problem: some dogs have narrowed nostrils, an elongated palate, or a collapsing trachea and they tire or cough out of proportion to the walk. A wiry coat should be stripped, not shaved bald.

Daily Norwich care is a short hunt-style walk, coat maintenance, and listening to the breathing. A dog that snores, gags, or fades on a mild day needs an airway exam, not a harder fitness plan. They dig and they bark at a rustle. That is the terrier, not a training failure on day one.
old-english-sheepdog: An Old English Sheepdog disappears under a heavy coat that has to be brushed to the skin or it mats into a pelt. They are a large herding dog, not a living stuffed animal, and hip dysplasia is the structural risk. Budget grooming time every week or pay a groomer who will not shave a neglected coat down to damaged skin.
pharaoh-hound: A Pharaoh Hound is a sighthound that blushes: the nose and ears flush pink when the dog is excited. They are lean, they chase anything that moves, and they can clear an ordinary fence. Anesthesia doses should respect a sighthound's low body fat. Give them a sprint and then a warm bed. Ribs that show are normal. A pot belly is not.
portuguese-water-dog: A Portuguese Water Dog is a working retriever with a curly or wavy coat that mats if it is not combed, and many are kept in a retriever clip. Juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy and GM1 gangliosidosis are genetic diseases to ask a breeder about by name. Hip dysplasia is the other screen. They need swimming or another hard job, not a weekend-only life.
puli: A Puli's coat is supposed to cord, and you do not brush cords the way you brush a collie. Separate the cords by hand so the skin can dry, or the dog mats into a solid felt. They are a herding dog under the hair, vocal and quick. Hip dysplasia is the orthopedic question. A shaved Puli is a welfare haircut, not a style.
pumi: A Pumi is a smaller Hungarian herder with a curly coat and a terrier-like bark. They need a job and a comb, and they will notify you about every leaf. They are not a quiet apartment ornament. Keep the coat from matting at the skin, and give the dog training that uses the brain or the barking becomes the hobby.
saint-bernard: A Saint Bernard is a giant, short-lived dog. Many are old by seven or eight. Gastric dilatation-volvulus, osteosarcoma, and hip disease are the expensive endings, and drool plus a large food bill start on day one. They do not belong in a hot apartment or up a flight of stairs every day. A gastropexy is a conversation to have at the spay or neuter, not after the stomach twists.
samoyed: A Samoyed's smile sits on a double coat that mats and overheats if you only skim the top. Brush to the skin, walk in the cool hours, and expect digging and barking. Hereditary glomerulopathy is the kidney disease to ask a breeder about before a puppy comes home. A Samoyed in a hot car or a noon run is a heatstroke risk.

Daily Samoyed work is the coat, a real walk, and a check of the skin under the ruff. They blow the undercoat and the house fills with hair. That is normal. Mats against the skin, a dog that pants in the shade, or a change in drinking and urine are not normal and need a person, not another day of waiting.
shiba-inu: A Shiba Inu is a primitive spitz that screams when restrained, sheds the undercoat in clumps twice a year, and often does not tolerate rude dogs. They are escape artists. A six-foot fence and a harness that cannot slip matter more than a cute photo. Same-sex aggression is common enough to plan the household before you add a second dog.
shikoku: A Shikoku is a rare Japanese hunting spitz, closer to a Shiba in temperament than to a retriever. They have a strong prey drive, a double coat, and an independent streak. They are a poor first dog if you want off-leash recall in a park full of squirrels. Find a breeder who will talk about hips, eyes, and temperament with the same detail they use for coat color.

Feed a Shikoku like a moderate athlete, not like a bulldog and not like a racing husky. They need a daily run on a long line or in a secure field, plus coat brushing when the undercoat blows. A Shikoku that is never allowed to hunt with its nose will hunt the cat.
skye-terrier: A Skye Terrier is a long, low dog under a floor-length coat. The back is the structural risk: disc disease and injury from jumping follow a long spine. The coat has to be kept from matting or the dog cannot move its legs freely. They are reserved with strangers and devoted to their person. This is not a drop-in greeting breed at the dog park.
soft-coated-wheaten-terrier: A Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier's silky coat mats easily and hides a more serious problem: protein-losing nephropathy and protein-losing enteropathy. Unexplained weight loss, vomiting, or a dog that drinks and urinates more needs blood and urine tests, not a diet trend. Comb the coat to the skin several times a week so mats do not become wounds.
tibetan-mastiff: A Tibetan Mastiff is a nocturnal livestock guardian. Barking at night is the job, not a phase. They are independent, suspicious of strangers, and large enough that an untrained adult is a liability. Hip dysplasia and a giant-breed lifespan, often under ten years, belong in the budget. They do not suit a house that wants a quiet evening or a dog that greets guests.
weimaraner: A Weimaraner is a velcro hunting dog. Separation anxiety is common and serious: a Weimaraner left alone for a full workday often destroys a door. They need hours of running. Hypertrophic osteodystrophy can hit growing pups as painful swollen legs, and bloat is the deep-chest emergency. Do not buy this breed for looks and a weekend hike.
welsh-corgi: A Pembroke Welsh Corgi is a dwarf herding dog, and the long back is why sofas and extra weight matter. Intervertebral disc disease can paralyze a dog that was jumping off the couch yesterday. Keep them lean, use a ramp, and do not encourage the jump. They herd children by nipping heels. That is instinct, and it needs training, not a laugh.

Daily Pembroke care is a couple of brisk walks, nail trims, and a body-condition check you can do with your hands. You should feel ribs. A corgi that is round is a disc injury waiting for a stair. Brush the double coat when it blows. They bark at the door because herding dogs comment on movement.

If a corgi suddenly cannot use the back legs, treat it as an emergency. Time matters for a disc extrusion. Do not wait out paralysis because the dog was walking that morning. Crate rest is a medical instruction after a vet has seen the dog, not a home guess.
wirehaired-vizsla: A Wirehaired Vizsla is a Hungarian hunting dog with a harsh coat that should be stripped, not shaved, and the same need to run as a smooth Vizsla. They are a rare breed. Hip and eye evaluations are the minimum ask of a breeder. A wire coat that is clipped repeatedly can lose the correct texture.

Plan a Wirehaired Vizsla day around exercise and company. They are not a kennel dog and they do not settle just because the yard is fenced. A hunt, a long trail run, or serious training is the outlet. The coat needs a weekly comb and a strip a few times a year so dead hair does not pack against the skin.
yorkipoo: A Yorkipoo mixes a Yorkshire Terrier's airway and teeth with a Poodle's coat, and neither size nor shedding is guaranteed. Collapsing trachea, dental disease, and patellar luxation are the Yorkie problems to watch in a dog this small. The coat mats if it is not combed to the skin. A toy dog that coughs when excited or pulls on a collar needs a harness and a vet, not a harder walk.
anatolian-shepherd: An Anatolian Shepherd is a livestock guardian that patrols and barks, often at night, and decides on its own what is a threat. They are independent and large. A suburban yard with close neighbors is a poor match. Hip dysplasia is the structural screen, and the dog needs a job guarding or a very serious handler, not a casual hike club.
australian-kelpie: An Australian Kelpie is a herding dog that will work until it drops and will herd the family if sheep are not available. They need intense daily exercise and training. They are not a laid-back companion. Heat, hips, and cerebellar abiotrophy in some lines are the health questions. A Kelpie in an apartment with one short walk will destroy the baseboards.
azawakh: An Azawakh is a West African sighthound, extremely lean, reserved with strangers, and fast enough to catch game. Ribs and hip bones show on a correct dog. They chill easily, they are sensitive to anesthesia, and they need a secure area for a sprint. They bond tightly and are a poor choice if you want a dog that greets every visitor.
belgian-tervuren: A Belgian Tervuren is the fawn, long-haired Belgian shepherd. The drive matches a Malinois more than a collie-mix photo suggests. They need work, they are often noise-sensitive, and epilepsy and hip dysplasia are the screening topics. Feed a performance diet in amounts that match actual work, not the appetite of a dog that would train all day.
boykin-spaniel: A Boykin Spaniel is a South Carolina hunting spaniel, smaller than a springer and just as insistent about work. Exercise-induced collapse has been identified in the breed, so a dog that wobbles and overheats after intense play needs a vet and a DNA conversation, not another ball. Hip and eye screens belong with the breeder. They are a poor couch-only dog.
brittany: A Brittany is a pointing dog that needs miles, not a lap. They are sensitive, birdy, and prone to getting lost on a scent if the recall was never proofed. Hip dysplasia and, in some lines, complement deficiency are worth asking about. A Brittany left alone with nothing to hunt will invent a search of the trash.
bullmastiff: A Bullmastiff is a guarding mastiff with a short muzzle, a heavy body, and a short lifespan. Airway noise, hip and elbow disease, and cancer, including lymphoma and osteosarcoma, dominate the later years. They overheat. They are not a jogging dog and not a breed for someone who has never trained a powerful guardian. Keep them lean from puppyhood.
chinese-shar-pei: A Chinese Shar-Pei carries a mutation that drives shar-pei fever: recurring fever and swollen hocks that can lead to amyloidosis and kidney failure. Wrinkled skin needs cleaning so folds do not infect, and entropion can scratch the eye. This is not a low-maintenance wrinkled companion. A fever episode is a vet visit, not a trait to wait out.
cocker-spaniel: A Cocker Spaniel's long ears and coat are the maintenance, and primary glaucoma, cataracts, and ear infections are the medical pattern. Heavy ear leather traps moisture. Dry the canals after a bath and do not pluck hair without a reason from a vet. They are a sporting spaniel: they need a walk and a job, and a cocker that head-shakes needs the ear looked at.
collie: A rough or smooth Collie needs a CEA eye status, an MDR1 drug-sensitivity test, and a promise you will not breed merle to merle. Ivermectin and several other drugs are dangerous in MDR1 mutants. The rough coat mats if it is not lined out. Collies herd motion and they are often sound-sensitive. Know the eye and drug status before you need them in an emergency.
dachshund: A Dachshund's long back and short legs are why intervertebral disc disease is the breed emergency. Jumping off furniture and extra weight are the levers you can actually move. There are three coats and two sizes. The wire coat needs stripping. A dachshund that suddenly drags the back feet needs a vet the same day, not a weekend of crate rest you invented.
doberman-pinscher: A Doberman needs a heart plan and a bleeding plan. Dilated cardiomyopathy is common enough that Holter monitoring and echocardiograms are adult maintenance, not a luxury. von Willebrand disease affects clotting. They are a velcro working dog that does not tolerate being parked in a yard. Wobbler syndrome and bloat are the other bills. Cropped ears are cosmetic, not a health need.
english-cocker-spaniel: An English Cocker Spaniel is a hunting spaniel, lighter and more work-oriented than many American cockers kept as pets. Rage syndrome, a rare sudden aggression linked in some lines to a genetic finding, and ear disease are the topics to raise with a breeder. They need exercise and coat care. A spaniel ear that smells sweet is yeast until proven otherwise.
finnish-lapphund: A Finnish Lapphund is a northern herding spitz with a thick coat and a barking habit that was useful around reindeer. They shed heavily, they need brushing to the skin, and they want a job or they comment on every sound. Progressive retinal atrophy and hip status are reasonable breeder questions. They are friendly and they are not a silent apartment dog.
jack-russell-terrier: A Jack Russell Terrier, or a Parson Russell if the dog is the taller standard, is a hunting terrier with more energy than the footage suggests. Primary lens luxation is the eye emergency: a suddenly painful, cloudy, or blue eye needs a vet the same day. They dig, they bark, and they do not retire. A small yard and a smart dog is not enough.
king-shepherd: A King Shepherd is a giant German Shepherd type developed in the United States, not a separate old breed with a closed health record. Size increases orthopedic and bloat risk, and the back-end weakness people see in shepherds does not improve by making the dog heavier. Ask what the parents' hips, elbows, and hearts actually did, and budget for a giant-dog food bill.
kishu-ken: A Kishu Ken is a Japanese hunting spitz, often white, with a strong prey drive and a reserved manner toward strangers. They are rare. They need a secure fence and a handler who does not expect Labrador recall around wildlife. Double-coat shedding is seasonal and heavy. Hip and eye information from the breeder matters more than a pedigree story.
komondor: A Komondor wears felted cords that take years to form and must be separated to the skin so air and water can reach it. They are a livestock guardian, wary of strangers, and large. Cords are not a cute trim: neglect becomes a mat that hides skin infection. Hip dysplasia and a guardian temperament are the other half of the decision. This dog barks at night on purpose.
kuvasz: A Kuvasz is a white Hungarian livestock guardian, independent and protective, not a fluffy retriever. They bond to their family and can be dangerous with strangers if that instinct is unmanaged. Hip dysplasia and a giant-breed lifespan belong in the plan. The white coat shows dirt and needs brushing, and the dog needs a job or a property, not a crowded dog park.
lagotto-romagnolo: A Lagotto Romagnolo is the Italian truffle dog, curly-coated and obsessive about scent work. The coat is never brushed like a collie. It is wetted and the curls are separated, or it mats. Juvenile epilepsy and a storage disease, Lagotto storage disease, are DNA tests to ask for. They need nose work. A walk without a job does not empty the battery.
maltese: A Maltese is a toy companion whose coat mats to the skin if it is missed for a week, and whose teeth rot if they are not brushed. Patellar luxation and portosystemic shunts, a liver bypass, show up in the breed. They are not a jogging dog. A Maltese that suddenly acts drunk, especially after a meal, needs a vet because of that liver shunt risk, not a theory about stubbornness.
miniature-pinscher: A Miniature Pinscher is a toy pinscher, not a deer-headed Chihuahua and not a calm lap ornament. They are bold, they bark, and they injure themselves jumping from furniture. Patellar luxation and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease affect the hind leg. Use a harness, watch the knees, and do not trust a Min Pin's confidence around big dogs or open doors.
neapolitan-mastiff: A Neapolitan Mastiff is a heavy guarding mastiff with loose skin, heavy drool, and a short life. Cherry eye, entropion, hip disease, and cardiomyopathy show up often enough to plan the vet fund before the puppy is purchased. Wrinkles need cleaning. They overheat. This is a guardian for an experienced home, not a wrinkly family dog from a movie.
plott-hound: A Plott Hound is a hunting hound with a voice that carries and a nose that does not turn off at the property line. They are athletic and they bay. A suburban quiet rule and a Plott are a poor match. Hip status and a secure fence matter. Hunting drive means a cat, a chicken, or a deer scent can erase the recall you practiced in the kitchen.
pointer: An English Pointer is a bird dog that ranges wide and needs miles of running. They are short-coated, lean, and miserable as a sedentary house dog. Hip dysplasia and, in some lines, inherited neurological disease are worth a breeder conversation. They chill in winter without a coat. A pointer that never gets to quarter a field will quarter the house.
presa-canario: A Presa Canario is a guarding mastiff from the Canary Islands, powerful and not a beginner breed. Many jurisdictions and insurers restrict them. Hip disease, a short mastiff lifespan, and a temperament that must be socialized on purpose are the decision. They are not rehabilitated by kindness alone. An experienced handler and a legal check come before a puppy deposit.
rat-terrier: A Rat Terrier is a farm hunting dog in a small body. They are bright, they dig, and they kill rodents, which is a problem if you also keep hamsters or birds. Patellar luxation and dental disease are the small-dog maintenance. They need a job and a secure yard. A Rat Terrier that is only walked around the block will make its own hunt indoors.
redbone-coonhound: A Redbone Coonhound bays, trails, and does not consider a leash a moral duty once a scent is fresh. They are a hunting hound with a loud voice and a short coat. Coonhound paralysis, polyradiculoneuritis, is an uncommon but breed-associated reason a hound suddenly weakens. A secure fence and a neighbor-tolerant plan for the bay are not optional.
schnoodle: A Schnoodle's coat, size, and shedding depend on which poodle and which schnauzer were used, and the adult can surprise you. Curly coats mat. Schnauzer-type dogs are prone to pancreatitis and to bladder stones, so a rich table scrap is a bad habit. Ask what the parents weighed and whether the coat was shaved or stripped. Groom to the skin on a schedule.
scottish-deerhound: A Scottish Deerhound is a giant sighthound, gentle and huge, with a lifespan often under ten years. Osteosarcoma, cardiomyopathy, and bloat are the diseases that end them, and anesthesia must respect a lean sighthound. They need room to stretch out and a soft surface for a large body. They are not a guard dog. They are a coursing dog that lives on the sofa between runs.
shetland-sheepdog: A Shetland Sheepdog is a small, sound-sensitive herding dog, not a miniature collie you can skip health tests on. MDR1 drug sensitivity, collie eye anomaly, and gallbladder mucocele are the Sheltie-specific problems. The double coat blows and mats. They bark. A Sheltie that is never given a job will herd the children and announce every truck.
shorkie: A Shorkie is a Shih Tzu and Yorkshire Terrier cross, usually a toy dog with a coat that mats and a face that does not cool itself well. House the dog in a crate tall enough to stand and long enough to stretch out, not a medium crate that becomes a bathroom. Use a harness. A collar yank on a tiny trachea is how these dogs cough.

Shorkie enrichment is short training, a food puzzle, and a supervised chew, not a marathon. They overheat and they bore easily. Ten focused minutes beat an hour of chaos. Keep hair out of the eyes, because a dirty face fold and long facial coat cause infections people mistake for allergies.

The expensive Shorkie problems are dental disease, patellar luxation, collapsing trachea, and eye irritation from facial hair. A dental cleaning on a toy dog is anesthesia, and it costs more than the puppy did. Brush teeth. A honking cough when the dog is excited is the trachea until a vet says it is something else.
spanish-water-dog: A Spanish Water Dog is a herding and water dog with a corded curly coat that is sheared once a year and not brushed. Brushing ruins the coat. They are intense, often wary of strangers, and they need work. Hip dysplasia and a storage disease, neuroaxonal dystrophy, are tests to ask about. A pet trim that leaves mats against the skin is not grooming.
spinone-italiano: A Spinone Italiano is a sturdy pointing dog with a wiry coat and a reputation for being calmer than a German shorthaired pointer, which is not the same as being a couch dog. Cerebellar ataxia is a fatal genetic disease with a DNA test. Ask for it. The beard holds water and needs drying or the skin infects. They need hours outside and a patient trainer.
standard-poodle: A Standard Poodle is a retrieving water dog under a clip. The coat mats to the skin if the schedule slips, and hip dysplasia, Addison's disease, and sebaceous adenitis are the medical trio to know by name. Bloat happens in deep chests. They need exercise and thinking work. A shaved-down neglected coat is a welfare haircut. Groom on a calendar, not when the dog is already felted.
thai-ridgeback: A Thai Ridgeback is a primitive guarding sighthound with a dorsal ridge and a strong opinion about strangers. The ridge is cosmetic. Dermoid sinus, a neural-tube defect along the spine, is the medical reason to have a vet palpate the midline. They are not a biddable retriever. Recall around prey is a lifetime project, and they do poorly when dumped at a dog park to make friends.
tornjak: A Tornjak is a large Balkan livestock guardian, independent and territorial, with a thick coat and a night bark. They are a rare guardian breed, not a fluffy companion. Hip disease, size, and a temperament that bonds to a property rather than to tricks are the decision. Neighbors who hate barking should end the conversation before a puppy is reserved.
welsh-springer-spaniel: A Welsh Springer Spaniel is a red-and-white hunting spaniel, active and usually friendlier off-switch than people expect, and still a spaniel that needs work. Primary glaucoma is the eye disease that can take vision quickly. A red, painful, or suddenly blind eye is an emergency. Ear infections follow wet floppy ears. They are not a rare-colored English springer. Ask for eye certifications.
welsh-terrier: A Welsh Terrier is a black-and-tan wire terrier that should be hand-stripped to keep the coat and the color. Shaving softens the jacket. They are a hunting terrier: they dig, they bark, and they are not finished at age two. Allergies and skin disease show up often enough to budget for a dermatology visit. They need a secure yard and a person who likes terriers.
wire-fox-terrier: A Wire Fox Terrier is a hunting terrier with a stripped coat and a sense of humor that includes excavation. They are not a quiet housedog. Deafness, lens luxation, and skin allergies appear in the breed. A suddenly painful eye is an emergency. The wire coat needs stripping a few times a year. A shaved wire fox is a different, usually worse, coat.
american-bobtail: An American Bobtail is a short-tailed cat, not a Manx. The tail is bobbed, not absent, and the spinal defect called Manx syndrome is not the same problem, but a short tail still deserves a vet who will look at the spine if the gait is odd. They are a large, dog-like, active breed. Hip dysplasia shows up in big cats. Give them climbing space and do not assume a bobtail is low maintenance.
arabian-mau: An Arabian Mau is a natural breed from the Arabian Peninsula, slim, heat-adapted, and vocal about territory. They are not a couch Persian. They need vertical space and a warm house, and they may not tolerate a rough introduction to other cats. Ask the breeder what the parents' hearts and kidneys actually did rather than buying a story about desert ancestry.
balinese: A Balinese is a long-haired Siamese: the same pointed pattern, the same voice, and the same need to be in the conversation. Progressive retinal atrophy, hepatic amyloidosis in related Oriental lines, and dental disease are the health pattern. The coat is single and silky, not a Persian mat, but it still needs combing. They do poorly as an ignored only-ornament cat. They want a person home.
bombay: A Bombay is a black cat bred to look like a miniature panther, built on Burmese lines. They are people-focused and they can inherit the Burmese problems: a head defect in some lines, hypokalemic polymyopathy, and a tendency toward diabetes. A Bombay that suddenly walks stiffly or cannot lift its head needs a vet the same day. They are not a low-shedding black domestic with a marketing name.
havana-brown: A Havana Brown is a rare solid-brown cat with a Siamese-family voice and a strong attachment to its person. They are not a low-interaction showpiece. Dental disease and respiratory infections show up, and a rare breed means you should ask what the parents died of, not only what color they were. They need play every day or they invent it at 2 a.m.
highlander: A Highlander is a curl-eared, often bobtailed hybrid cat, large and active, developed from Desert Lynx and Jungle Curl lines. The ear curl and the short tail are mutations. Ask whether the parents were curl-to-curl bred and whether anyone has tracked cartilage or spinal problems. They need space to climb. A hybrid look is not a care plan, and the adult size can surprise a person who bought a kitten photo.
khao-manee: A Khao Manee is a Thai white cat that often has odd eyes, one blue and one gold, and the blue eye can come with deafness on that side. Test hearing rather than assuming a white cat is ignoring you. They are an old natural breed, social and not a Persian. Sunburn is a risk on white ears. A deaf cat must be kept indoors because it cannot hear a car or a dog.
lykoi: A Lykoi is a werewolf-look cat caused by a sparse-coat mutation. The skin is not a costume: it needs monitoring for sunburn, oiliness, and lesions, and the cat may look moth-eaten when the coat cycles. They are a mutation breed, not a healthy barn cat in costume. Ask what skin workup the breeder actually does, and keep them indoors out of strong sun.
nebelung: A Nebelung is a long-haired blue cat developed to resemble a long-haired Russian Blue. The coat is the work: comb it so it does not mat, especially behind the ears and the trousers. They are usually reserved with strangers and devoted to their own people. Ask about hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the heart disease that matters in many pedigreed cats, before you treat the breed as a low-risk blue domestic.
sokoke: A Sokoke is a rare East African forest cat with a blotched tabby coat and a lean, active body. They are not a sedentary apartment ornament. They climb and they can be shy. Because the breeding population is small, ask about the parents' health and the degree of inbreeding rather than buying rarity alone. Give them height and hiding places.
thai: A Thai cat is the traditional, rounder-headed pointed cat from which the extreme modern Siamese was developed. They are still vocal, social, and people-dependent. They should not be left as a sole ornament while everyone works fourteen-hour days. Dental disease and the old Siamese issues, including amyloid risk in related lines, are worth asking about. A quieter voice than a show Siamese is not a guarantee.
turkish-van: A Turkish Van is a swimming, high-energy cat with a waterproof-feeling coat and a reputation for being busy. They are not a lap Persian. Some like water. All of them need climbing and play or they rearrange the house. Deafness can accompany a white coat, so test it. Heart screening is reasonable in any pedigreed cat you expect to keep into the teens.
american-wirehair: An American Wirehair's coat is crimped by a mutation. It should feel springy, not matted, and it needs a comb rather than a heavy bath routine. They are a rare American breed, usually sturdy, and the adult is a normal-sized cat. The health file is thin because the breed is small, so buy from someone who can tell you what the parents died of, not only how the coat feels.
asian: An Asian cat, in the British sense, is a Burmese-derived solid or tabby, not a random domestic from Asia. They are people-oriented and can inherit Burmese metabolic problems, including hypokalemia and a risk of diabetes. A cat of this type that becomes weak in the neck or drinks excessively needs bloodwork. They want company and play, and they are not a low-interaction roommate.
birman: A Birman is a pointed, long-haired cat with white gloves. The coat mats if the trousers and tail are ignored, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the heart disease to screen for in pedigreed cats. They are usually quieter than a Siamese and still social. A Birman that suddenly cannot use the back legs may be throwing a clot from heart disease. That is an emergency, not a sprain.
british-longhair: A British Longhair is the long-coated version of the cobby British Shorthair. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and polycystic kidney disease are the screens that matter, and the coat needs combing so the dense undercoat does not felt. They are often calm and they are still a cat that needs play. A round face and a thick coat overheat in a hot room. Keep them lean. Extra weight hides the ribs and stresses the heart.
british-shorthair: A British Shorthair is a cobby, dense-coated cat. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the disease that kills apparently fine cats, so a murmur or a sudden hind-limb paralysis is an emergency. Polycystic kidney disease has occurred in the breed. They are calm, not inactive. Keep them lean, because a thick coat hides weight gain until the cat cannot groom.
chartreux: A Chartreux is a blue French cat with a woolly double coat and a quiet voice. They are sturdy and they hunt. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and patellar luxation are the medical questions. The coat sheds the undercoat seasonally and needs combing then, not shaving. A Chartreux that stops eating is a cat emergency like any other, because hepatic lipidosis follows a few days of anorexia.
colorpoint-shorthair: A Colorpoint Shorthair is a pointed cat recognized separately from the Siamese in some registries, with the same voice, the same social need, and the same dental and eye pattern. They are not a low-maintenance color variant. Crossed eyes and a kinked tail are not charms to breed for. Give them company and a vertical space, and treat a sudden change in drinking as a vet visit.
cornish-rex: A Cornish Rex has a short wavy coat and very little hair to protect the skin. They chill easily, they burn, and they are a high-metabolism cat that eats a lot for its size. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and patellar luxation show up. They are acrobats. A Cornish Rex needs warmth and play, and a bald belly is normal. Bald patches with crusts are not.
devon-rex: A Devon Rex has a fragile, pixie coat and large ears, and the breed carries a hereditary myopathy that causes muscle weakness, especially in the neck, and a risk of laryngeal spasm under stress. They also get hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A Devon that cannot hold its head up needs a vet. They are people-obsessed and they chill easily. This is not a sturdy barn cat in a cute coat.
domestic-longhair: A domestic longhair is a mixed-breed cat with a long coat, not a pedigree. The useful facts are the ones you can see: weight usually in the 8 to 15 pound range, a lifespan often into the teens if the cat is indoors, and a coat that mats if nobody combs it. Dental disease, obesity, and not knowing the parents' hearts are the real risks. Comb to the skin and keep the cat inside.
european-shorthair: A European Shorthair is a pedigreed version of the ordinary European street cat, bred to a standard but still a robust shorthair. They need ordinary cat care done properly: indoor life, a dental check, and a weight you can feel. Because they are bred, ask about hypertrophic cardiomyopathy rather than assuming a natural look means no heart disease. They play. A bored adult still knocks things off shelves.
korat: A Korat is a silver-blue Thai cat with a heart-shaped face and a strong attachment to its people. They are a rare breed with known gangliosidosis, a storage disease with a DNA test, and a risk of the same heart problems seen in other pedigreed cats. Ask for that test. They do not like rough change. A Korat is a commitment to one vocal, sensitive cat, not a blue domestic from a shelter list.
peterbald: A Peterbald is a Russian hairless or brush-coated cat developed with Oriental and Don Sphynx lines. Bare skin needs washing, sun protection, and warmth. They are a high-energy Oriental type: vocal, social, and miserable if ignored. Dental disease is common in the Oriental family. A hairless cat that is greasy or has pustules needs a skin plan, not another sweater.
ragdoll: A Ragdoll is a large pointed cat bred to go limp when held, which is a temperament claim, not a reason to skip heart screening. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the disease that matters, and a cat this big hides weight under a soft coat. They are usually gentle and they are still cats that need play and a slow introduction to dogs. A Ragdoll that suddenly loses the back legs may have thrown a clot.
russian-blue: A Russian Blue is a short, dense blue cat, usually reserved with strangers and attached to its own people. They are not a high-groom breed, but they do shed the undercoat. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and dental disease are the medical maintenance. They stress when the routine changes. A Russian Blue that hides and stops eating needs a vet quickly, because cats develop fatty liver disease after only a few missed meals.
scottish-fold: A Scottish Fold's folded ear is cartilage disease, osteochondrodysplasia, and it hurts. Every folded cat has some degree of it. Fold-to-fold breeding makes crippling arthritis more likely. A straight-eared cat from fold lines can still carry the gene. This is not a cute ear shape with a normal skeleton. Pain control and a breeder who only folds to straight ears are the minimum ethical bar.
serengeti: A Serengeti is a spotted cat bred from Oriental and Bengal lines to look like a serval without being a wild hybrid. They are active, lean, and vocal. They need height and play. Ask how many generations from any wild ancestor and what heart screening the Oriental side received. A look-alike serval is still a house cat with a high drive, and it will not be quiet.
siamese: A Siamese is a vocal, social, pointed cat that does not tolerate being an ignored ornament. Dental disease, progressive retinal atrophy, and, in related Oriental lines, hepatic amyloidosis are the health pattern. They want a companion person or another cat and a vertical territory. A Siamese that is suddenly quiet and fluffed is sick. The breed's normal voice is loud. Silence is the alarm.
somali: A Somali is a long-haired Abyssinian, ticked, active, and busy. The coat needs combing and the cat needs play. Pyruvate kinase deficiency, progressive retinal atrophy, and renal amyloidosis are the Abyssinian-family diseases to ask about by name, and DNA tests exist for the first two. A Somali that drinks a lot or loses weight needs a kidney workup, not a theory about being picky.
toyger: A Toyger is a striped cat bred to look like a toy tiger, developed from Bengals and domestic shorthairs. They are active and people-oriented. The stripes are not a wild animal. Ask about hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and what the Bengal side was screened for. They need play and scratching posts that survive a determined cat. A designer stripe pattern does not change litter-box or dental care.
alexandrine-parakeet: An Alexandrine Parakeet is a big Asian ringneck, larger and louder than the Indian ringneck people think they bought. They need a flight cage, hours out, and a pellet-and-vegetable diet, not a seed hopper. They scream and they bond to one person. Psittacine beak and feather disease and bornavirus are the infection questions for any new parrot. A seed-only diet is how these birds get vitamin A deficiency.
coturnix-quail: Coturnix quail are ground birds, not parrots and not a child's handheld pet. They startle upward and can break their necks on a low ceiling, so housing should be low and soft-topped or tall enough that a flush does not hit wire. They need grit, a game-bird diet, and deep bedding. Eggs are the point for many keepers. Handling a quail every day is how you stress it to death.
diamond-dove: A Diamond Dove is a tiny Australian dove, smaller than a ringneck dove, and it frightens easily. They do better as a pair you watch than as a bird you clutch. They need a long flight cage, a fine-seed and pellet mix, and grit or a cuttlebone for calcium. Cold drafts and a cat in the same room are the usual disasters. A puffed, still dove is a sick bird, not a calm one.
dusky-conure: A Dusky Conure is one of the smaller Aratinga conures, green with a dark head, and it is still loud for an apartment. They need a roomy cage, time out, and a pellet diet with vegetables. They chew. A seed-only diet and a shoulder that is all the enrichment they get produces a screaming, biting bird. Annual exams with an avian vet matter because a sick conure hides illness until it is thin.
mynah: A Common Mynah is a starling, a softbill, not a seed-eating finch. Fruit, insects, and a low-iron softbill diet are the food. Iron storage disease is the reason you do not feed a mynah a high-iron pellet meant for another bird. They mimic and they are messy. They need a large aviary space. A mynah on a parrot-seed mix is being malnourished.
owl-finch: An Owl Finch, or Bicheno finch, is a tiny Australian grassfinch that should be kept as a pair or a group, not as a handling pet. They startle and they do not want to sit on a finger. Give them a long flight cage, mixed finch seed plus egg food and greens, and no draft. A finch on the cage floor, fluffed, is an emergency. These birds decline in hours.
rosellas: Rosellas are Australian parrots, and several species get sold under one name. Crimson, eastern, and pale-headed rosellas are not the same size. They need space, a pellet and vegetable diet, and they can be aggressive toward other birds. Import and state law matter for Australian parrots. A seed-only rosella becomes obese and vitamin-A deficient. Ask which species is actually in the cage.
spice-finch: A Spice Finch, the scaly-breasted munia, is a small social finch. Keep them in a group, in a flight cage, on a finch-seed mix with greens and egg food. They are not a hand-tame parakeet. Drafts, a single bird, and a diet of only millet are the usual failures. Watch the droppings and the weight. A finch that sits fluffed on the floor needs heat and an avian vet the same day.
button-quail: Button quail, the Chinese painted quail, are ground birds the size of a golf ball. They need a low enclosure so a flush does not break a neck, a fine game-bird or finch diet, and grit. They are not a pet to hold. Females can exhaust themselves laying. A heat lamp used carelessly cooks them. If you want a bird that sits on a finger, this is the wrong species.
cape-parrot: A Cape Parrot is a rare South African parrot, not a generic amazon. They are associated with yellowwood forest and they are not a beginner cage bird. Beak and feather disease and respiratory infection matter, and any Cape Parrot in trade should have paperwork you can actually read. They need a large cage, a pellet and produce diet, and an avian vet. Wild-caught or smuggled birds are a legal and a welfare problem.
conure: Conure is a group, not a species. A green-cheek and a sun conure differ in noise by an order of magnitude. Before you budget food or insurance, name the species. All of them chew, all of them need pellets and vegetables rather than a seed diet, and all of them need hours out of the cage. A conure screaming every evening is often under-slept or bored. Twelve hours of dark, quiet night is the first fix.
gouldian-finch: Gouldian finches are colorful Australian finches that do badly in a dirty, drafty cage. Air-sac mites are the classic illness: a bird that clicks when it breathes or bobs its tail needs an avian vet, not a new toy. Keep them warm, in a group, on a finch mix plus egg food and greens. A Gouldian on the cage floor is an emergency. These birds hide sickness until they are nearly gone.
green-wing-macaw: A Green-wing Macaw is one of the giant macaws, close to a hyacinth in presence and louder than a person expects from a photo. They live for decades, they chew furniture, and they need a room-sized space and a diet of pellets, vegetables, and some nuts, not a bucket of sunflower seed. Beak and feather disease testing and a legal source matter. This is not a step up from a cockatiel.
hyacinth-macaw: A Hyacinth Macaw is the largest flying parrot, a specialist on hard palm nuts, and a decades-long commitment. They need a huge space, a diet built around nuts and pellets rather than fat alone, and a vet who has seen one. CITES controls the trade. A hyacinth is a poor first parrot and a poor apartment bird. The beak can destroy a wall and a finger with the same casual bite.
indian-ringneck: An Indian Ringneck is a slim Asian parakeet that screams, bonds hard, and can become a one-person biter at maturity. They need a long flight cage, out-of-cage time, and a pellet diet. Seed-only birds develop vitamin A deficiency and respiratory disease. Ask whether the bird is captive-bred. A talking ringneck is still a loud parrot, and the talking does not replace foraging.
jenday-conure: A Jenday Conure is a loud Aratinga, orange and green, and it is a poor secret in an apartment. They need hours out, things to destroy, and a pellet-and-vegetable diet. They bite when they are hormonal or under-slept. Budget the noise and the chew toys before the color. An avian vet visit once a year, and sooner if the bird is fluffed or thin, is the health plan.
lineolated-parakeet: A Lineolated Parakeet is a small, quieter parrot than a conure, often called a linnie. They still need a flight cage, a pellet and vegetable diet, and company. They are not a silent decoration and they are not a budgie with better manners guaranteed. Seed-only diets make them fat. A linnie that stops flying up to the perch is sick until an avian vet says otherwise.
macaw: Macaw is several species. A noble or a Hahn's macaw is not a scarlet, and the food bill, the noise, and the legal paperwork scale with the bird. All macaws chew, all of them live for decades if they are the large species, and all of them need pellets, produce, and foraging rather than a seed diet. Buy the species you can house at adult volume, not the baby that is quiet in the shop.
moluccan-cockatoo: A Moluccan Cockatoo is a large salmon-colored cockatoo with a scream that is a welfare problem in the wrong house. They need hours of direct attention, a huge cage, and a diet that is not just sunflower seed. They pluck when bored or hormonal. This is one of the parrots most often rehomed. Powder-down and noise are daily facts. A plucked Moluccan needs a medical workup, not only a new toy.
peach-faced-lovebird: A peach-faced lovebird is a small parrot with a disproportionate bite and a loud voice for its size. They need a flight cage, pellets and vegetables, and either a compatible mate or a person who is actually home. A mirror is not a friend. They can become egg-bound if they lay repeatedly. Nesting behavior, a bird on the cage floor, or a swollen abdomen needs an avian vet.
pigeon: A domestic pigeon is a flock bird that needs a loft or a large flight, a seed mix made for pigeons, and grit. They are not a parrot and they are not dirty by nature if the loft is managed. Salmonella and respiratory disease spread in crowded, wet lofts. One pigeon kept alone in a small cage is a welfare problem. Plan the mess, the flock, and a vet who will see a bird.
princess-parrot: A Princess Parrot is an Australian parakeet, slim and long-tailed, and it is not a quiet budgie. They need a long flight cage, a pellet and vegetable diet, and room to fly. Australian species may be restricted where you live. Seed-only birds become obese. A princess parrot that sits fluffed or stops flying needs an avian vet. The tail is a furnishing they break in a short cage.
red-factor-canary: A red-factor canary is a color canary, and the red comes from carotenoids in the diet during molt, not from a dye poured on the feathers. They need a canary seed mix, greens, cuttlebone, and a cage wide enough to hop. They are not a handling pet. Drafts and a dirty cage floor cause the respiratory disease that kills canaries. Color food is optional. Clean air is not.
red-rumped-parrot: A Red-rumped Parrot is an Australian grass parrot. They spend time on the ground, they can be aggressive toward other birds, and they need a flight cage and a pellet, seed, and green diet. State law may restrict Australian parrots. They are not a shoulder bird. A red-rump that is fluffed on the cage floor needs heat and an avian vet. Obesity from an all-seed diet is the common chronic problem.
society-finch: Society finches are domestic mannikins bred to foster other finches, and they should live in a group. They are not hand-tame and they stress when grabbed. Give them a flight cage, a finch mix, egg food, and greens. A single society finch is a welfare failure. Drafts, mites, and a diet of only millet are the usual reasons they die. A fluffed bird on the floor is an emergency.
star-finch: A Star Finch is a small Australian grassfinch. Keep them in a pair or a group, in a long flight, on finch seed plus greens and egg food. They are not a petting bird. Cold and drafts kill them faster than a missed treat. Air-sac mites and a dirty cage are the disease risks. If you want a bird that talks or sits on a shoulder, buy a different order of bird.
sun-conure: A Sun Conure is one of the loudest common parrots for its size. The color is the sale. The scream is the ownership. They need hours out of the cage, things to shred, and a pellet-and-vegetable diet. They bite during hormonal season. An apartment with shared walls is often the wrong building. A sun conure that is quiet and fluffed is sick. The healthy one is the noisy one.
toucan: A toucan is a softbill with a huge beak and a diet problem: iron storage disease. They need a low-iron softbill diet, fruit, and no high-iron pellets or citrus in the amounts a parrot would get. The cage has to be huge and padded because they injure that beak and their hips. This is a specialist bird, a mess, and a poor pet for someone who wanted a colorful parrot. Find a vet before the bird.
abyssinian-guinea-pig: An Abyssinian guinea pig is a cavy with a rosette coat, not a low-maintenance hamster. The whorls mat if they are not combed, and the animal still needs unlimited grass hay, vitamin C every day, and a friend. Guinea pigs do not make their own vitamin C. A pig off its hay, or one that squeaks when it urinates, needs a vet who treats exotics.

Daily Abyssinian care is hay, a vitamin C source that is not a sugary treat, a cage big enough to run, and a comb through the rosettes. They are crepuscular and they popcorning is normal. A limp, a head tilt, or diarrhea is not. Keep them in same-sex pairs. A single guinea pig is a lonely herd animal, not a simpler pet.
chinchilla-mutations: Chinchilla color mutations are still a chinchilla: a dense-coated, heat-intolerant rodent that needs a dust bath, a large multi-level cage, and hay. Temperatures much above the mid-70s Fahrenheit can kill them. Fur chewing and dental disease are the common problems. A color name does not change the diet. No fruit snacks, no cedar, and no wheel with a small solid back that kinks the spine.
chinchilla-standard-gray: A standard gray chinchilla is the wild-type coat, and the care is the same as any pet chinchilla. Unlimited grass hay, a measured pellet, a dust bath several times a week, and a temperature that stays cool. Dental malocclusion shows up as drooling and a wet chest. Heatstroke shows up as a flat, hot animal. Both are emergencies. They are not a cuddly hamster, and they live 10 to 15 years when the teeth and the heat are managed.
chinese-hamster: A Chinese hamster is a small, fast, often solitary hamster, not a dwarf that wants a roommate. They are escape artists and they bite when grabbed. Give them a deep cage, a solid wheel, and a seed-and-pellet mix with protein. Diabetes and a short life, often around two years, are the expectation. Housing two together because a care sheet said hamsters are social is how these ones get injured.
degu: Buy a pellet labeled for degus, or a high-fiber hay-based pellet that does not list molasses, honey, or dried fruit in the first ingredients. Hay is the food. A yogurt drop, a raisin, or a fruit mix is the usual reason a degu develops cataracts and diabetes. By the time the eye clouds, the sugar has already done the damage.
emperor-scorpion: An emperor scorpion is a moist-forest invertebrate, not a desert pet. They need a deep damp substrate, a hide, and a temperature that does not cook them under a badly placed heat lamp. They eat insects, not fruit. The sting is usually compared to a bee, which is still a reason to know whether anyone in the house is allergic, and they should not be handled as a toy. A dry tank is how emperors die.
fancy-rat: A fancy rat's plan is lungs, friends, and a cage that breathes. Mycoplasma is nearly universal, so a rat that gasps or loses weight needs a vet who will use rat-safe antibiotics, not a pet-store drop. Keep at least a same-sex pair, skip wire floors, and avoid aquariums that trap ammonia. Females grow mammary tumors often enough that a new lump should be seen, not watched for a month.
giant-african-land-snail: A giant African land snail is often illegal to own, import, or move across state lines in the United States because it is an agricultural pest. Check the law before you buy a shell in a shop. If you are somewhere they are legal, they need a humid tank, cuttlebone for calcium, and a plant diet. A cracked shell is a calcium and humidity failure. This is not a harmless classroom novelty.
mongolian-gerbil: A Mongolian gerbil is a desert rodent that needs a deep sand bath and a deep cage for tunnels, and it should live in a same-sex pair that was raised together. They are illegal to keep as pets in California. Scent glands on the belly are normal. A wet tail, a head tilt, or a seizure is not. They chew plastic. Give them wood, cardboard, and a wheel with a solid surface.
rex-guinea-pig: A Rex guinea pig has a short, dense, curly coat that still needs checking for skin problems, plus the same non-negotiables as any cavy: unlimited hay, daily vitamin C, and a companion. The Rex coat does not protect them from scurvy. A pig that hops instead of walks, or drools, needs a dental and vitamin check. Keep the cage large and the bedding dry so the short coat does not sit in ammonia.
rex-rabbit: A Rex rabbit has a plush coat with guard hairs the same length as the undercoat, and the skin is more exposed to pressure sores if the rabbit sits on a wet or wire floor. They need hay as the main food, a large pen, and a companion or serious daily contact. Dental disease and GI stasis are the emergencies. A rex that stops eating is not being picky. It needs a rabbit vet the same day.
american-rabbit: An American rabbit is a large breed with a mandolin body and a semi-arch, not a dwarf lop. Adults are heavy. They need a pen measured in feet, not a pet-store cage, unlimited grass hay, and nail trims. Sore hocks happen on wire floors. GI stasis, a rabbit that stops eating and defecating, is an emergency. Budget space and a rabbit-savvy vet before the purchase price.
angora-rabbit: An Angora rabbit is a wool breed. The coat mats into a pelt that pulls on the skin if it is not groomed several times a week, and wool block can kill a rabbit that swallows its own hair. Hay must be the staple. A matted Angora is a welfare problem, not a busy week. Daily grooming, a large pen, and a vet who understands GI stasis are the cost of the coat.
baldwin-guinea-pig: A Baldwin guinea pig is a hairless cavy. The skin needs a warm room, protection from sun and scrapes, and the same vitamin C and hay as any guinea pig. Hairless does not mean low maintenance. They chill, they sunburn, and they still need a companion and a large cage. A Baldwin off its food needs vitamin C and a dental check, because scurvy and teeth are still the cavy emergencies.
english-angora: An English Angora carries furnishings on the face and ears and a coat that will felt if you skip grooming. Wool block from swallowed hair is the emergency: a rabbit that stops eating needs motility drugs and fluids from a rabbit vet, not a wait. Hay is the diet. The coat is a daily chore. If you cannot groom on a schedule, do not buy the wool.
fennec-fox: A fennec fox is a wild canid, not a small dog. Many states and cities ban them, and even where they are legal they mark, scream at night, and do not housetrain like a dog. They need a large secure space, a diet that is not kibble alone, and a vet who will see an exotic canid. The ears are for heat, and a fennec in a cold spare bedroom is the wrong animal. Check the law first.
ferret-sable: A sable ferret is the ordinary color of the domestic ferret, not a different species. They need a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet, hours out of a multi-level cage, and a vet who knows insulinoma and adrenal disease, the two illnesses that dominate middle-aged ferrets. They are illegal in California and restricted elsewhere. A ferret that is weak, staring, or drooling may be hypoglycemic. Rub honey on the gums and go to a vet.
flemish-giant: A Flemish Giant is a rabbit that can pass 15 pounds. The cage sold for a dwarf will cripple it. They need a pen big enough to hop, unlimited hay, and a floor that does not cause sore hocks. GI stasis and dental disease are still the emergencies, and the food bill matches the size. A Flemish that stops eating needs a rabbit vet the same day. This is livestock-scale care with a pet's lifespan.
hairless-rat: A hairless rat is a fancy rat without a coat. The skin needs a warm room and checks for scratches and oil, and the rat still needs a friend, a ventilated cage, and a vet for respiratory disease. Mycoplasma does not care that the rat is bald. They chill easily. Do not house them on dusty bedding that irritates bare skin. A gasping hairless rat is the same emergency as any other rat.
hissing-cockroach: A Madagascar hissing cockroach is a large insect that needs a warm, humid tub, hiding bark, and a diet of vegetables and a protein source. They are not a sterile classroom toy: they can live for years, the males ram each other, and some people are allergic to cockroach proteins. They are restricted in a few places. A dry, cold tank is how they die. They do not need a heat lamp sitting on the lid.
mini-rex: A Mini Rex is a small Rex rabbit, not a dwarf hamster. The plush coat and the exposed skin mean they need a clean, solid floor and hay as the staple. Dental disease and GI stasis are the emergencies. A mini rex that is small enough to live in a pet-store cage is still a rabbit that must hop. Give a pen, a friend or daily contact, and a vet who treats rabbits before the first weekend of soft stools.
mouse: A fancy mouse lives about one to two years, needs a same-sex group if they are females, and produces a lot of ammonia in a small tank. Males often fight. Give them a wheel, deep bedding, and a pellet made for mice, not a seed mix that lets them pick out the fat. Respiratory disease is the common killer. A mouse breathing with its mouth open is dying. See a vet the same day.
netherland-dwarf: A Netherland Dwarf is a brachycephalic rabbit. The short face contributes to dental malocclusion, tear-duct disease, and a higher anesthetic risk. They need hay, a pen, and a companion plan. They are not a starter rabbit because they are small. A dwarf that drools or has a wet eye needs a dental exam. GI stasis is still an emergency. Budget the vet, not only the hay.
prairie-dog: A prairie dog is a colonial rodent, not a ground squirrel you can keep in a hamster cage. They need deep substrate to dig, a specialized diet low in the junk sold as treats, and a vet who understands odontomas, the tooth tumors that block their airways. They are banned or restricted in many states. They bark, they chew, and they can carry zoonoses. Check the law before the animal.
roborovski-hamster: A Roborovski hamster is the smallest and fastest pet hamster, about two inches long, and a poor choice if you want to hold a pet. They startle, they bite when grabbed, and they need a large cage with deep bedding and a solid wheel. They can live around three years, which is long for a hamster. Housing them with a slower species, or in a tiny colorful cage, is how they get injured.
texel-guinea-pig: A Texel guinea pig is a long-haired curly cavy. The coat mats and collects urine if it is not trimmed and combed, and the animal still cannot make vitamin C. Hay, a daily vitamin C source, a large cage, and a companion are the care. A fancy coat does not change scurvy, dental disease, or the need for a dry bed. A Texel that is left unbrushed becomes a welfare case under its own hair.
bamboo-shrimp: A bamboo shrimp is a filter feeder. It fans the current and starves in a still, too-clean tank with nothing suspended to eat. Breeding them in a home aquarium almost never works because the larvae need saltwater conditions the adult tank does not provide. Give them flow, a mature tank, and supplemental powdered food if the water is too polished. A shrimp that never fans is hungry.
blue-green-chromis: A blue-green chromis is a schooling marine damselfish. One fish in a nano tank is the wrong plan. They need a group, swimming room, and stable saltwater parameters. They are hardy for a marine fish and they still die in a new, uncycled tank. Aggression shows up if the group is too small or the tank is too short. Buy the school, quarantine them, and do not add them to a tank that is still cycling.
cardinal-tetra: A cardinal tetra is a soft, acidic-water schooling fish from the Rio Negro, and it fades in a small, alkaline, unplanted tank kept too warm and too dirty. Keep them in a group of at least eight, in a cycled tank, and do not confuse them with the hardier neon if your water is liquid rock. They are not a beginner fish just because they are small and cheap. A single cardinal hiding in a corner is a stressed fish.
cleaner-shrimp: A cleaner shrimp will pick at a fish's parasites and at your fingers, and it will be eaten by many fish people put in the same tank. It needs a mature saltwater system, stable salinity, and iodine in the normal reef range, not a bottle poured in at random. Molting is when they are vulnerable. A cleaner shrimp in a brand-new tank, or with a hungry wrasse, is a snack.
common-pleco: A common pleco grows past a foot and a half and produces a remarkable amount of waste. It is not an algae solution for a ten-gallon tank. Adults need a large cycled aquarium, driftwood to rasp, and a diet that includes vegetables and algae wafers, not fish waste. They live for years. The usual story is a baby bought for algae control that outgrows the tank and pollutes it.
dwarf-gourami: A dwarf gourami is a labyrinth fish that breathes at the surface and is commonly infected with iridovirus, which is why so many die within months of purchase. Buy from a source with a quarantine habit, keep the tank warm and covered, and do not house two males together. They are not a hard fish to feed, and they are a hard fish to keep alive if the shipment was already sick. A gourami that sits at the top gasping in a dirty tank needs a water change and a diagnosis.
endler-livebearer: An Endler's livebearer is a tiny poeciliid, not a guppy you can neglect, though the two hybridize if you mix them. They need a cycled tank, hard water, and plants, and the females will produce fry if a male is present. They are poor community-tank targets for anything with a mouth big enough to eat them. A heater, a lid, and a group matter more than a fancy color name.
rasbora: Rasbora is a group of small schooling cyprinids. A harlequin and a chili rasbora do not want the same tank: chilies need soft, warm, planted water and a tight school, and they die in a hard, bare community tank. Keep the species you actually bought in a group, in a cycled aquarium, and do not add them during a cycle. A single rasbora hiding is a social and a water-quality failure.
swordtail: Swordtails are omnivores with a preference for plant matter. They also need a lid, because they jump, and a tank long enough for a male to display the sword without being nipped to pieces. Livebearing means a female can drop fry you did not plan to raise. Keep males from harassing one female into exhaustion. A swordtail in a ten-gallon with three males is a fight, not a display.

Feed a swordtail a flake or pellet that is not pure protein, plus blanched greens. They tolerate a range of hard water and they do not tolerate a filthy one. Ich, fungus on a nipped fin, and a female that is bullied until she hides are the common problems. Quarantine new livebearers. A shop swordtail often arrives with parasites and a pregnancy.
bangai-cardinal: A Banggai cardinalfish is a mouthbrooder that should be captive-bred if you can find one, because wild collection hit the species hard. They are slow, they get bullied, and they need a calm saltwater tank with hiding places. Do not house them with fast, nippy fish. A Banggai that is thin is often being outcompeted at feeding time. Target-feed it. Stable salinity matters more than another ornament.
dottyback: A dottyback is a small, aggressive marine fish. An orchid dottyback will eat ornamental shrimp and harass tankmates that cannot fight back. They need a lid, a cave, and a tank that is not a peaceful reef soup. Research the species: some are worse than others. They are useful against bristleworms and terrible with a cleanup crew you like. A dottyback in a ten-gallon with a shrimp is a shrimp obituary.
why-is-my-dog-not-sleeping: A dog that paces at night, pants at rest, or cannot lie down needs an exam, not a later bedtime. Pain, a full bladder, canine cognitive dysfunction in seniors, and airway trouble are common reasons. See a specialist when the regular vet has treated pain and the pacing is still every night, or when there are seizures, collapse, or breathing effort at rest.
why-is-my-cat-not-using-litter-box: A cat that suddenly misses the box needs a urine test before a behavior theory. Cystitis, crystals, and arthritis, when the box is too high or too far, cause more house-soiling than spite. Scoop daily, keep one box per cat plus a spare, and skip scented litter while you are ruling out a medical cause. Blood in the urine or a male cat straining is an emergency.
manx-cat-pet-insurance: Manx syndrome is a spinal and nerve defect in tailless Manx cats, and it is the condition that decides whether a policy is worth buying. Ask whether congenital disease and spinal surgery are covered, and enroll before a vet writes a gait problem into the record. A tailless kitten with an already-noted spine defect may be excluded for the only illness you were insuring against.
fish-nutrition: Flake food loses vitamins within months of the tub being opened, and a carnivore flake will starve a pleco or an otocinclus that needs algae and vegetables. Match the food to the fish: herbivores get greens and algae wafers, carnivores get a meaty frozen or pellet food, and color comes from carotenoids plus clean water, not from dye on the label.
guides: Use a comparison when it names the difference that will change your week: exercise minutes, grooming, noise, and the disease that actually generates the vet bill. The links below are head-to-heads. Popularity is not a care plan, and a winner on a chart is the wrong animal if you cannot do the work on an ordinary Tuesday.
dogs: The guides linked here are breed-specific on purpose. An exercise page for a malamute is about heat and a freight dog's joints. An exercise page for a terrier is about a hunt drive. Open the page that names the dog you have, and ignore a recommendation that would fit every breed on the list.
